cur:catacombs2-perugia-san-bernardino-sa.summary: Seven niches divided by columns hold standing figures, and at the centre Christ sits enthroned among them, flanked by a personification of the Church and the apostles. On the lid, small Old Testament scenes, including Noah's ark and Jonah, speak of death and rebirth around a central inscription panel. Reused as the altar of the Renaissance oratory, it now holds the remains of Blessed Giles, companion of Saint Francis.
facts: Italian Wikipedia attributes it to the same workshop as the famous sarcophagus of Junius Bassus in the Vatican Grottoes.
It was previously kept in the crypt of the neighbouring church of San Francesco al Prato.
cur:catacombs2-perugia-san-bernardino-sa.notes: The photographer's Commons description reads the central scene as Christ the Teacher or a form of the Traditio Legis.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, haloed and holding a cross-staff, sits on a green globe and reaches out to a kneeling bearded man, while a young man stands at the right and further figures crowd below. The psalm's closing verses proclaim that 'all the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:objects2-coin-romanos-i-constantine-.summary: Christ sits enthroned on a lyre-backed throne, blessing and holding the Gospel book, surrounded by the inscription IHS XPS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who rule'. On the other face the senior emperor Romanos I Lekapenos appears with the young Constantine VII, the legitimate Macedonian heir whom he had pushed into second place.
facts: The figure of Christ returned to Byzantine gold coinage after the end of Iconoclasm, and the enthroned type became a standard reverse of the Macedonian period.
Romanos I seized power in 919–920 as father-in-law of the boy emperor Constantine VII, and co-emperors of his own family soon displaced Constantine on the coinage.
cur:objects2-coin-romanos-i-constantine-.notes: Distinct from the Romanos I and Christopher issue already in the collection (cur:objects-coin-romanos-i-christopher-solidus); the museum's date range covers the whole reign.

cur:objects2-quintanilla-de-las-vinas-re.summary: On this carved block two winged angels, their robes rendered in parallel grooves, fly toward a central frontal bust with large almond eyes, long hair and a beard, holding a fold of drapery. The church of Santa María de Lara is celebrated for containing what is often called the earliest image of Christ in Spanish art, and this block is commonly associated with that identification. Its flat, linear style is one of the most distinctive voices of Visigothic sculpture.
facts: The church is generally dated to the late 7th or early 8th century, though some scholars have placed it as late as the 10th century.
It was declared a national monument on 25 November 1929, after being rediscovered by a local priest in 1921.
Two other reliefs, depicting Evangelists, were stolen in 2004 and recovered in a British garden in 2019 by the Dutch art detective Arthur Brand.

cur:objects2-quintanilla-de-las-vinas-re.notes: Sources disagree on which block depicts Christ: some locate the Christ bust above the keystone of the arch, others among the loose blocks inside; a second loose block shows a beardless bust holding a cross between angels. The identification of this bearded bust as Christ could not be confirmed from a scholarly catalogue.

Q18719519.summary: At the center, Christ's body is laid in the tomb by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus as Mary bends over him and angels display the instruments of the Passion. On the left wing a donor kneels before the empty cross on Calvary; on the right Christ rises from the tomb. Set against a richly tooled gold ground, the triptych stands at the very beginning of Early Netherlandish oil painting, combining medieval splendour with a startling new realism.
facts: It is named after Count Antoine Seilern, who bequeathed it to the Courtauld on his death in 1978.
It is generally attributed to Robert Campin, the teacher of Rogier van der Weyden, and is the earlier of the two triptychs associated with him.
Its elaborately tooled gold background is a survival of older Gothic panel practice, even as the figures are painted with the new oil technique.

Q977200.summary: God the Father stands behind the crucified Christ, supporting the cross, while the dove of the Holy Spirit hovers between them; Mary gestures toward her Son and John gazes up in prayer. The scene is set in a coffered, barrel-vaulted chapel painted with such convincing linear perspective that it seems to open a real space in the church wall. It is one of the first great works of the Renaissance and a landmark in the depiction of Christ within a rational, measurable world.
facts: It is among the earliest surviving paintings to use systematic one-point perspective, likely inspired by Brunelleschi's experiments and perhaps made with his advice.
Below the altar a painted skeleton bears the inscription 'I was once what you are, and what I am you also will be.'
The kneeling donors, painted roughly life-size just outside the painted chapel, seem to share the viewer's own space — a striking innovation.
Around 1570 Vasari built a new altar in front of the fresco, concealing it; the upper part was rediscovered in 1860, and the skeleton below only in the 20th century, the two being reunited in 1952.

Q567861.summary: Covering the entire altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, the fresco shows Christ as a powerful, beardless judge at the centre of a vast whirl of more than three hundred figures, raising the blessed to heaven and casting the damned down. The Virgin turns beside him, and saints surround him bearing the instruments of their martyrdom. It is a vision of awe and reckoning painted in the aftermath of the Sack of Rome and amid the Reformation.
facts: It was commissioned by Pope Clement VII and completed under Pope Paul III.
Saint Bartholomew holds his own flayed skin, whose distorted face is widely believed to be Michelangelo's self-portrait.

After the Council of Trent, Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint draperies over many nude figures, mostly after Michelangelo's death in 1564, earning the nickname 'Il Braghettone' (the breeches-maker).
A major restoration completed in 1994 revealed a far richer range of colour, including the deep blue of the sky, than had been visible for centuries.
